title: Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Cycles
book_title: Chapter 1: Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Cycles
question: How was the business built, and what did each stage do to revenue, margins and cash?

epigraph.quote: “Move commodities from farmers gate to consumers table.”
epigraph.author: Proventus Agrocom Ltd, company website home page

web_blocks.html: Proventus Agrocom has rebuilt its business model more than once in eleven years. Each rebuild reset revenue, margin and cash in a different way, and the latest one has not yet run through a full year. We trace four operating regimes: commodity bulk trading to FY2020, the brand pivot of FY2021–FY2022, the brand scale-up of FY2023–FY2026, and the manufacturing build-out that began in FY2027. Dates and figures come from the prospectus, annual reports and exchange filings [10][3][1].

The company was incorporated in Mumbai on 20 October 2015 as Manthan Agrocom Private Limited. It was renamed Proventus Agrocom within two months and became a public company in March 2023 [10]. Its first stated object was commodity broking, trading and hedging, including derivatives, across agricultural products, metals and energy. Agriculture came second [10].

The two operating founders are commodity-desk people. Durga Prasad Jhawar, the managing director and CEO, is a chartered accountant with more than 26 years in the field and was managing director of Edelweiss Commodities. Deepak Kumar Agrawal, the whole-time director, ran Aster Commodities DMCC in Dubai. CFO Ankush Jain came from Edelweiss Treasury [3]. A third promoter, Shalin Khanna, left in 2025. A Dubai commodity entity followed in May 2016 [10]. These are traders who learned to run a factory and a brand, not brand managers who learned to trade.

web_blocks.title: Regime one: bulk trading and the FY2020 loss

web_blocks.html: In the prospectus the company says it began by “undertaking bulk trades” in agro produce from the Navi Mumbai wholesale market, importing almonds from California and Australia [10]. By FY2020 consolidated revenue was ₹896.2 crore. Bulk sales of other commodities were ₹474.9 crore (53.0%), bulk and white-label dry fruits were ₹385.4 crore (43.0%), and the ProV brand was only ₹35.05 crore (3.9%) [10]. This was a trading house with a small brand attached.

FY2020 ended with a restated EBITDA of –₹21.67 crore and a loss after tax of ₹21.90 crore [10]. The prospectus gives the cause. Derivative positions in commodities lost ₹19.26 crore when the Covid lockdown halted trade and international prices fell. The company also held a large stock of unsold goods at that point, since inventory of stock in trade rose by about ₹173 crore in the year, and finance cost was ₹11.24 crore [10]. The loss equalled 44% of the ₹49.8 crore net worth that remained at year-end [10]. A thin-margin book of ₹900 crore can lose a large part of its capital on one bad price move, and the pivot to branded goods set out to remove that risk.

web_blocks.title: Regime two: the deliberate shrink into brand

web_blocks.html: FY2021 revenue fell 66% to ₹300.9 crore. The fall was chosen, not forced. Bulk and white-label sales dropped 71% from ₹861.2 crore to ₹250.5 crore, the company discontinued its agri-commodity business, and derivative activity was cut back [10]. ProV brand sales rose 42% to ₹49.8 crore. Finance cost fell 93% to ₹0.81 crore because the credit lines were barely used [10]. The business made a ₹1.88 crore profit, and EBITDA margin moved from –2.4% to about 1.0%.

The legal structure was built for this pivot. Prov Foods Private Limited, the brand and manufacturing subsidiary, was incorporated on 25 November 2019. Proventus Retail dates to December 2015, the Dubai commodity entity to 2016, and the Pro-Nova Bio Technologies shell to October 2020 [10]. The Mumbai plant lifted packing from 40,000 to 60,000 pouches a day around 2021–2022, then moved from Mahape to Khairane after a vacate notice in January 2023 [10]. Sources disagree on the ProV launch year: the prospectus says 2017, the website 2016, and the FY2026 annual report timeline implies 2019. We use 2017 [10][3].

web_blocks.html: Between 2015 and 2020 the entity was a trading company with a side brand. From 2022 the dates cluster around capital, people and plants: an IPO, a promoter exit, an auditor change and two factories. Each of those events carries a governance or execution question that later chapters weigh.

web_blocks.title: The endorsement deal and the subsidiary web

web_blocks.html: The November 2022 endorsement agreement with Chef Sanjeev Kapoor and KS Narayanan, amended in March 2023, was paid largely in equity and warrants of Prov Foods rather than cash [10]. That is why the listed parent now owns 98.75% of its main operating subsidiary and not 100% [3]. The structure saved cash in a year of thin margins, and it hands the endorsers a small slice of Prov Foods’ future profit. Proventus Retail has no turnover, Pro-Nova Bio is a 51% shell, and the Dubai entity lost ₹0.18 crore in FY2026 [3]. In economic terms the group is two companies, the parent and Prov Foods, which chapter 2 separates.

web_blocks.title: The IPO: what was promised and what was done

web_blocks.html: The March 2023 draft was book-built; the April draft and May final prospectus were fixed-price [12][11][10]. The issue was 9,02,000 shares at ₹771, worth ₹69.54 crore. Fresh shares were 6,71,853, raising ₹51.80 crore. The offer for sale was 2,30,147 shares worth ₹17.74 crore, which went to the sellers, chiefly the promoter LLP (1,02,147 shares) and Guruprasad Rao (95,001 shares) [10]. About a quarter of the issue was therefore not company money. After ₹1.25 crore of issue expenses, net proceeds to the company were ₹50.55 crore.

web_blocks.html: Almost 60% of the raise was earmarked for the subsidiary and went there as an internal loan, which the parent still carries and earns interest on (₹1.32 crore in FY2026) [3]. About ₹15 crore has been repaid. No monitoring agency was needed because the issue was below ₹100 crore, so the use of funds rests on the company’s own statement [23]. Nothing in the filings suggests misuse. It does show that the IPO money financed working capital, not plants, and that the parent became the bank for the brand business.

web_blocks.title: After the IPO: exits, slippage and open claims

web_blocks.html: Shalin Khanna, a named promoter and whole-time director, resigned on 22 May 2025 “to pursue other opportunities and interests” [29]. The CEO called it personal reasons [9]. He was reclassified from promoter to public by September 2025 and holds 3.07% [21]. The promoter holding fell from 70.45% to 67.34% as a result, so the decline is reclassification, not open-market selling [3][21].

The auditor change is the second flag. NBT & Co was appointed in February 2023, re-approved in August 2023 for five years, and resigned on 26 December 2025, about 2.3 years into that term. Its letter cites a “strategic focus on specialised certification and advisory engagements” and bandwidth for a larger audit [26][16]. Chechani Soni & Co audited FY2026 with an unmodified opinion and no key audit matters, and was re-appointed in September 2026 [3][27]. We see no evidence of a dispute, but a mid-term exit by the auditor of the IPO-era accounts is worth weighing beside the cash-flow record.

Surat is the clearest case of execution slippage. In September 2024 the CEO said the new plant was “set to be up and running by the end of the year” [19]. In May 2025 the target became the end of FY2026 [9]. Phase 1 was declared ready in July 2026 and “completed and operational” in November 2026, at a Phase 1 capex of ₹14 crore [7][2]. That is roughly 22 months after the first promise. Capacity promises also moved, from 8 lakh units a day in the filing, to 4 lakh at the AGM, to 5 lakh pouches on completion [25][19][2]. Phases 2 and 3, with cold storage, are now due by June 2027 [2].

Two claims remain open. The Bihar makhana unit was announced in May 2026 at 2,500 tonnes a year, but a July 2026 press release says it is being “progressively expanded” towards that figure over three years [8][7]. A secondary summary of the May 2026 call says the CFO aims to migrate to the NSE main board by the end of FY2027, and we found no filing that shows an application [42]. Both stay unproven.

web_blocks.title: Revenue, margin and cash across the cycles

web_blocks.html: Brand share rose from 4% to about 72%, yet the margin barely moved. EBITDA margin on management’s basis, which includes other income, moved from –2.4% to a band of roughly 1.8% to 2.6% and has stayed there since FY2023 [10][15][3][1].

web_blocks.caption: Consolidated revenue, profit and cash by year; ₹ crore
web_blocks.takeaway: Sources: prospectus [10]; annual reports [15][3]; H1 FY27 results [1][2]. FY2021 and FY2022 operating cash flow is from a third-party data feed [67]; FY2023 EBITDA is our calculation. H1 FY27 is unaudited.

web_blocks.html: Revenue grew 30% a year from FY2023 to FY2026, and brand revenue more than tripled, but profit did not follow the mix. Our own arithmetic on the audited lines shows reported gross margin rising from 7.2% in FY2023 to 9.9% in FY2026 and 12.0% in H1 FY27 [15][3][1]. EBITDA margin rose only about 30 bps over the same span. Selling, people and brand costs took the gross gain. Cash tells the same story: cumulative operating cash flow for FY2023 to FY2026 was +₹0.7 crore against ₹32.5 crore of cumulative profit [15][3]. The loss of cash in H1 FY27 was –₹57.6 crore, and net cash of about ₹19.6 crore at March 2026 turned to net debt of about ₹51 crore at September 2026 by our arithmetic [1]. Management says H1 builds stock for the festive second half, and FY2026 did reverse H1 [2][3]. Whether FY2027 does the same is not yet known.

web_blocks.the_number: About 70% of FY2026 consolidated revenue, roughly ₹645 crore of ₹925 crore, is genuine consumer-brand sales. Management reports 71.2%.
web_blocks.how_calculated: Management’s ProV brand revenue is ₹659 crore against consolidated revenue of ₹925.0 crore, which is 71.2%. We then haircut about ₹14 crore at the midpoint and up to ₹60 crore at the low end, because the company does not say whether brand revenue is net of trade promotion or includes co-packed or institutional ProV-labelled sales.
web_blocks.the_inputs: Brand revenue ₹659 crore (annual report and FY2026 presentation) [3][5]. Consolidated revenue ₹925.0 crore [3]. In H1 FY27 the split adds up exactly: ₹456 crore brand plus ₹177 crore white-label and bulk against ₹633.3 crore consolidated [2][1]. The FY2026 deck shows FY2025 brand revenue of ₹492 crore, while the annual report and the May 2025 call give ₹417 crore, an 18% gap in the same series [5][3][9].
web_blocks.the_range: 65% to 71%, that is ₹600 crore to ₹659 crore. The low end assumes about 9% of reported brand revenue is institutional or co-branded.
web_blocks.if_off: If the full ₹659 crore is consumer-pack revenue, the share is 71% as reported. If the low end is right, about ₹325 crore of revenue is still trading-type, and the 2% margin owes more to the base business than to the brand.

web_blocks.title: Definitions to hold in mind
paragraphs: Management reports a 22.1% ‘gross margin’ for FY2026 and ₹75 crore of ‘marketing investment’. The audited statements show a 9.9% gross margin on materials and purchases, and a marketing, advertising and promotion line of ₹20.2 crore [5][3]. This chapter uses only audited lines for margin and cash.

web_blocks.html: The evidence supports a clear story on origin: a commodity desk that lost money in bulk, shrank on purpose, built a brand to 71% of sales, and raised small IPO money that mostly funded the subsidiary. It does not yet prove that brand scale lifts the margin, that plant build-out can be funded from operating cash, or that management can keep to its dates.

web_blocks.title: How the stock has traded: past price cycles

web_blocks.html: Since the NSE Emerge listing on 5 June 2023 the shares have completed one full cycle and started a second. The issue price was ₹771, the first close was ₹862.05, and the 2023 intraday high of ₹1,348.80 came on 21 June, within three weeks [10][73]. The closing low of the year was ₹845.00 on 28 September, and 2023 ended at ₹1,000. The tape is thin, with a median of 320 shares a day over the last 250 sessions, so these are closing prints and not a deep market verdict [73].

The first peak was a closing high of ₹1,876.35 on 24 September 2024 (intraday ₹1,890), one day after Prov Foods announced the purchase of the Surat site [25][73]. The trough followed. By 11 August 2025 the close was ₹915.00, a fall of 51.2% over 321 days, and the intraday low of ₹815.10 came on 2 September 2025. That decline ran through the year in which EBITDA of ₹12.92 crore fell short of the ₹22 crore an analyst said had been guided, a promoter-director resigned, and operating cash flow stayed negative [9][29][15]. The closing price regained the 2024 peak on 17 August 2026, 371 days after the trough. By 12 November 2026 the stock was up 54.4% for the year and 66.2% over twelve months.

web_blocks.html: The price path follows the operating story more closely than a thin tape would suggest. The 2024 peak came with the Surat announcement and a year in which brand share reached 61%. The long decline matches the EBITDA miss against the guide, the promoter exit and negative cash flow. The recovery began once FY2026 delivered revenue of ₹925.0 crore, profit of ₹14.3 crore and positive operating cash flow, and Surat was reported ready. Governance events moved the price modestly: the Khanna window rose 4.9% and the auditor window fell 3.9%. Operating news moved it more. The stock has already fallen by half once when delivery slipped, which frames the unproven claims that close this chapter.

book_paragraphs: Let me start with a question I ask about every company with a brand on the shelf. Where did the people who run it learn their trade? Here the answer is the commodity desk. Durga Prasad Jhawar ran Edelweiss Commodities. Deepak Agrawal ran Aster Commodities in Dubai. Their company was born as Manthan Agrocom in October 2015 and its first stated object was commodity broking and hedging. Agriculture came second. A dry-fruit pouch was nowhere in the paperwork.

Picture the early business. A trader sits in the wholesale market at Navi Mumbai, takes in almonds that came off a ship from California, and sells them by the tonne to wholesalers. The margin per kilo is thin, but the volume is big. By FY2020 the company turned over ₹896 crore this way. More than half of it was other commodities entirely, not dry fruit. The brand it had started called ProV made ₹35 crore, under 4% of the total. If you had walked the floor then, you would have called it a trading house.

Then the lockdown arrived. The prospectus is blunt about what happened. Commodity prices fell worldwide, the company’s derivative positions lost ₹19.26 crore, and it was holding a pile of unsold stock. The year ended with a ₹21.9 crore loss, which was 44% of the net worth that remained. Andy Grove titled a book Only the Paranoid Survive, and a thin-margin trading book that big is where that advice earns its keep. I read the next move as a decision about risk, not about marketing.

What did the company do? It shrank on purpose. In FY2021 revenue fell by two-thirds to ₹301 crore. Bulk and white-label sales dropped 71%. The agri-commodity business was discontinued. Interest cost fell 93% because the credit lines went unused. And the company made a small profit of ₹1.9 crore. Ask yourself what it takes for a management team to give up two-thirds of its revenue to make money. It takes real conviction, or real fear, and probably both.

The rebuilt business lives mostly in a subsidiary called Prov Foods, incorporated in November 2019. The parent buys and sells nuts, and Prov Foods flavours, packs and brands them. I want you to keep that picture in mind because chapter 2 depends on it. In FY2022 the brand made ₹77 crore, and by FY2023 about ₹212 crore, half of all sales. A chef endorsement came in November 2022, paid largely in subsidiary equity and warrants, so cash stayed in the business. The listed parent today owns 98.75% of Prov Foods for that reason.

Why does the endorsement structure matter to you? Because it shows how this management behaves when cash is tight. A celebrity chef and a respected business name sit on the pack, and both were paid mostly in paper. A founder who protects cash that way is careful. The same founder, as you will see, also lent most of the IPO money downward and kept a single subsidiary at the centre of everything. Care and concentration are two different habits, and this company has both.

Then came the IPO in May 2023. Nine lakh shares at ₹771, about ₹70 crore in all. A quarter of it was sellers cashing out, and the company kept ₹50.5 crore after costs. Here is a detail you should not skim past. Of that, ₹29.86 crore, almost 60%, was lent to Prov Foods that same June. So the parent raised the money and handed most of it down to the subsidiary that actually runs the brand. About ₹15 crore has come back. The filings show no deviation, and nothing in them looks improper. But it tells you the IPO funded working capital, not factories.

After that, the story gets bumpier. A promoter and whole-time director, Shalin Khanna, resigned in May 2025 “to pursue other opportunities and interests”, and is now classed as public. The statutory auditor resigned in December 2025, about two years into a five-year term, citing a “strategic focus on specialised certification and advisory engagements”. I do not read either as a scandal. But you and I should log them, because small events like these are where a pattern begins.

And then Surat. In September 2024 the CEO told his AGM the new plant “is set to be up and running by the end of the year”. In May 2025 he said it “should be up and running by the end of Financial Year ’26”. Phase 1 was declared ready in July 2026 and complete in November 2026. That is a slip of roughly 22 months on the first promise. Plant dates in food manufacturing do slip, so I would not be harsh. What I would do is write down that this management has been early with its promises and late with its deliveries.

The makhana story belongs here too. In May 2026 the company announced a 2,500-tonne plant at Purnia in Bihar, the state that supplies most of India’s fox nuts. Two months later a press release described the same plant as being expanded towards that capacity over three years. Which is it? The filings do not say, and I would not pretend to know. I would simply mark it as a fact to verify, and I would do the same for the plan to move from the SME board to the main board by the end of FY2027, which rests on a secondary summary of a call and on no filing.

Now to the part that I think matters most. Look at what four regimes did to the numbers. In the bulk era the margin was negative and the balance sheet carried loans and stock. In the pivot the margin turned slightly positive and the company needed almost no financing. In the scale-up, from FY2023 to FY2026, revenue grew 30% a year and brand revenue more than tripled, yet EBITDA margin only moved from about 1.9% to 2.1%. The gross margin we compute from the audited statements climbed from 7.2% to 9.9%, and the people and brand costs took nearly all of it. Over those four years the business earned ₹32.5 crore of profit and ₹0.7 crore of operating cash.

The newest regime is manufacturing. Surat and a makhana plant in Bihar are meant to cut costs and widen the range. The first half of FY2027 shows what building costs: operating cash flow of –₹57.6 crore, receivables doubled since March, and a net cash position of about ₹20 crore turned into net debt of about ₹51 crore. Management says the first half always builds stock for the festive half and points to FY2026, when cash did flow back. The CEO’s own letter in November 2026 concedes the point, saying that growth requires “the ability to convert earnings into healthy cash flows over time”.

One last discipline. When I ask how much of this revenue is truly brand, management says 71%. I would say about 70%, with a range of 65% to 71%, because the company has never defined brand revenue in a way an outsider can test, and its own decks disagree by 18% on FY2025. So the origin story is clear and the proof is partial. A trading desk became a brand company in about five years. Whether it has also become a cash-generating one is the question every later chapter has to answer.

Before we leave the history, let me show you how the shares have behaved, because the price tells its own story about these four regimes. The company listed in June 2023 after a ₹771 issue, and within three weeks the shares touched ₹1,349. Then they drifted back to ₹845 by September. A first rush, followed by a first doubt. It is the pattern of a new listing with few shares changing hands, and I would not read much into it.

The real arc starts in September 2024. The company had just bought the land in Surat, the brand was 61% of sales, and the shares closed at ₹1,876. Then the year went wrong in ways you now know. The EBITDA guide was missed, a promoter director resigned, and cash kept leaking. By August 2025 the closing price was ₹915, down 51% in 321 days, and on 2 September the intraday low touched ₹815. Notice what that fall was not: it was not a collapse in the business. Revenue was still growing. It was a loss of trust in delivery, and trust takes longer to rebuild than it does to lose.

It took 371 more days for the shares to close above the old peak, which they did on 17 August 2026. In between, the auditor resigned, the stock shrugged, and the FY2026 numbers and the first Surat plant did the repair work. By 12 November the stock was up 54% for the year. When you look at that line, remember what it is a picture of: a company whose promises slipped, then partly arrived. Whether the next promises arrive on time is the question the rest of this book keeps asking.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A business that gives up two-thirds of its revenue to stop losing money has shown it can choose discipline over size. A business that earns ₹32.5 crore of profit and ₹0.7 crore of cash in four years has shown it has not yet chosen discipline over growth. Both facts belong to the same management team, and you should keep them side by side.
